clinical_knowledge.topic: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.
Standard management emphasizes immediate restriction from competitive sports and high-intensity athletics pending specialist review, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: chest tightness and lightheadedness while playing competitive football

Key HPI features: Presents after experiencing severe lightheadedness, tunnel vision, and central chest tightness during a competitive football match yesterday. Reports three similar episodes of exertional pre-syncope and shortness of breath over the past 6 months. Never fainted completely. Family history is notable: his paternal uncle died suddenly at age 26 while playing basketball (cause unexplained).

Objective/Exam findings: Cardiac auscultation: ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal border that characteristically INCREASES in intensity with Valsalva manoeuvre or standing up from squatting (due to decreased preload reducing left ventricular volume and increasing dynamic outflow tract obstruction), and decreases with squatting or passive leg raise. ECG: deep dagger-like Q waves in inferior and lateral leads, left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. Transthoracic echocardiogram (shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy >15mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve - SAM).
Relevant background/PMH: mild childhood asthma, no prior cardiac investigations
Current medications: salbutamol inhaler PRN before exercise
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Vasovagal syncope without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Syncope during exercise, or a family member who died suddenly and young.
management_principles: Immediate absolute restriction from competitive sports and high-intensity athletics pending specialist review
Consider beta-blocker therapy (e.g., bisoprolol or metoprolol) after specialist assessment to slow heart rate, improve diastolic filling, and reduce dynamic outflow obstruction
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: chest tightness and lightheadedness while playing competitive football

Presents after experiencing severe lightheadedness, tunnel vision, and central chest tightness during a competitive football match yesterday. Reports three similar episodes of exertional pre-syncope and shortness of breath over the past 6 months. Never fainted completely. Family history is notable: his paternal uncle died suddenly at age 26 while playing basketball (cause unexplained).
reference_soap.objective: Cardiac auscultation: ejection systolic murmur at the left sternal border that characteristically INCREASES in intensity with Valsalva manoeuvre or standing up from squatting (due to decreased preload reducing left ventricular volume and increasing dynamic outflow tract obstruction), and decreases with squatting or passive leg raise. ECG: deep dagger-like Q waves in inferior and lateral leads, left ventricular hypertrophy with strain. Transthoracic echocardiogram (shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy >15mm, systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve - SAM).
reference_soap.assessment: Hypertrophic Obstructive Cardiomyopathy (HOCM). DDx: exercise-induced asthma, anomalous origin of coronary arteries, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy (ARVC), ion channelopathy (Long QT syndrome).
reference_soap.plan: Immediate restriction from competitive sports and high-intensity athletics pending specialist review. Consider beta-blocker therapy (e.g., bisoprolol or metoprolol) after specialist assessment to slow heart rate, improve diastolic filling, and reduce dynamic outflow obstruction. Avoid unnecessary preload reduction with diuretics or nitrates in obstructive physiology. Urgent referral for cardiac MRI, 48-hour Holter monitoring to detect non-sustained ventricular tachycardia, and clinical genetic testing/counselling for first-degree relatives. Assess for Implantable Cardioverter Defibrillator (ICD) primary prevention.

learning_objectives: Correlate exertional syncope in young athletes with hereditary structural/electrical heart disease (HOCM, ARVC, Long QT)
Demonstrate understanding of dynamic auscultation: why HOCM murmur louder on Valsalva/standing and softer on squatting
Explain the physiological rationale for beta-blockers and the need to avoid unnecessary preload reduction in obstructive HCM
Perform comprehensive family history screening for sudden unexplained cardiac death under age 40

teaching.one_liner: A genetically thickened heart muscle obstructs outflow during exercise — the classic cause of collapse in a young athlete.
red_flags: Syncope during exercise, or a family member who died suddenly and young

must_ask.objective: Symptoms during rather than after exercise
must_ask.say: Did this happen while you were actually playing, or afterwards?
Has anyone in your family died suddenly and unexpectedly, especially young?
Have you felt lightheaded or actually blacked out?
Do you get chest tightness when you push yourself hard?
Does your heart ever race or thump on its own?
What sport do you play, and how many hours a week?

history.answer: Yesterday while playing football, my chest felt really tight and I got so dizzy that my vision started tunneling.
It hit me suddenly yesterday about 30 minutes into my football match while I was sprinting down the wing.
The tightness was right in the center of my chest behind my breastbone, covering a broad area rather than a single spot.
It felt like a heavy, constricting pressure or a tight band squeezing around my chest, not sharp or stabbing.
No, the tightness stayed right in the middle of my chest and did not spread to my jaw, left arm, neck, or back.
It lasted about 5 to 10 minutes until I sat down and rested on the bench, and I have had three similar episodes over the past 6 months.
At its worst during that sprint, I would rate the pressure around a 6 out of 10.
It definitely happens right in the middle of hard running, not after the match is finished.
Running hard definitely brings it on, and sitting quietly on the sideline makes it gradually fade away.
No, taking a deep breath, coughing, or leaning forward did not change the tightness at all.
It has no relation to food, and I have never had heartburn, sour burps, or trouble swallowing.
I felt severely lightheaded and everything went dark around the edges like tunnel vision, but I caught myself before completely passing out.
My heart was pounding very hard and fast in my chest, though I assumed that was just from sprinting.
Yes, I became very winded and couldn't catch my breath when the chest tightness started.
I was sweating from playing, but I did not have sudden cold sweats, nausea, or vomiting.
No, I haven't had any fever, chills, cough, or mucus at all.
No, I haven't had a cold, sore throat, or body aches recently.
Neither of my legs is swollen or sore, and I haven't been on any long flights or had surgery.
No, I haven't noticed any rash, bumps, or blisters on my chest or anywhere else.
I wasn't feeling panicked before it started, though I got really frightened once my vision went dim.
I haven't taken a blow to the chest, and I haven't done any heavy bench pressing recently.
I play semi-professional football and train intensely five days a week, plus match days on weekends.
I don't have high blood pressure, diabetes, or high cholesterol, and I have never smoked.
No, I have never had an ECG, an echocardiogram, or any heart tests done before.
I had mild asthma when I was a child, but otherwise I've always been completely healthy.
I have never had any surgeries or needed to stay in a hospital.
I only use a blue salbutamol inhaler once in a while before training, and I don't take any other pills or supplements.
No, I don't have any known allergies to medicines.
I have never smoked cigarettes or vaped, and I don't use any recreational drugs.
I don't drink any alcohol at all.
I'm a university student playing semi-pro football, living in a flat with university roommates.
My paternal uncle died suddenly at age 26 while playing basketball, and no one ever figured out why.
I figured I was just getting dehydrated and pushing myself too hard in high-intensity games.
I'm terrified because my uncle died so young during a game, and I'm at the same age now.
I'd like a complete heart checkup so I know whether it's safe for me to continue playing competitive football.

exam.finding: Blood pressure is 118/76 mmHg, pulse 68 beats per minute and regular, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 99% on ambient air, and body temperature 36.7 degrees Celsius.
Well-developed, athletic young male in no acute distress; skin is warm and dry with no pallor or diaphoresis.
Jugular venous pressure is not elevated, measuring approximately 2 cm above the sternal angle at 45 degrees with normal waveforms.
Symmetrical chest wall without deformities; no tenderness on palpation and a sustained apical impulse is felt in the fifth intercostal space.
Resonant to percussion bilaterally across all lung fields.
Normal vesicular breath sounds bilaterally with no wheezes, crackles, or pleural rubs.
Harsh crescendo-decrescendo ejection systolic murmur best heard at the left lower sternal border that increases in intensity with Valsalva and standing, and decreases with squatting.
Brisk, bifid carotid upstrokes palpable bilaterally, with symmetric radial and femoral pulses and no delay.
Abdomen is soft, non-tender, and non-distended, with no guarding, rebound, or palpable organ enlargement.
Both calves are symmetrical, supple, and non-tender, without swelling or palpable venous cords.
No pitting or non-pitting edema in either lower extremity.
Skin is clear and intact without rash, petechiae, or visible lesions.
